Kunětická hora Castle
Kunětická hora Castle (Czech: hrad Kunětická hora) is a castle in the municipality of Ráby in the Pardubice Region of the Czech Republic. The castle lies on Kunětická hora Hill, about 6 km from the city of Pardubice. The castle played an important role during the Hussite Wars of the early 15th century, as a fortress of Diviš Bořek of Miletínek. Today the castle is open to the public as a museum.
History
[edit]
In 1491 it was bought by Vilém of Pernštejn, who had the castle rebuilt in the late Gothic style, with two towers and a moat. The construction was continued by Vilém's sons in the early Renaissance style. During the Thirty Years' War, in the early 17th century, the castle was besieged several times; at the end of the war, Swedish troops burned it to the ground.
The castle remained a ruin until the early 20th century, when the Pardubice Museum Society was formed. The group purchased the site in 1919 and began reconstruction in 1923, according to the plans of architect Dušan Jurkovič. The rebuilding was completed in 1996.
Present
[edit]
Today the castle is open to the public as a museum. On display are surviving murals, including a 1523 work depicting Samson and Delilah, the oldest known Renaissance mural in Bohemia. The castle also hosts occasional music or theatrical performances.

Kunětická hora Castle is a striking medieval fortress located near Pardubice in Bohemia, Czechia. Perched on an isolated volcanic hill, the castle dominates the surrounding countryside and offers panoramic views across the Elbe lowlands. Its distinctive silhouette and historic fortifications make it one of the most recognizable landmarks in eastern Bohemia.
| Kunětická hora Castle, Bohemia, Czechia | 
The castle was established in the late 14th or early 15th century and gained strategic importance during the Hussite Wars. It was later expanded by the influential Pernštejn family, who strengthened its defenses and developed the complex. After periods of damage and decline, restoration projects helped preserve its architectural heritage.
Today, Kunětická hora Castle is a popular destination for travelers interested in medieval history, Czech architecture, and scenic landscapes. Visitors can explore its courtyards and fortifications, discover stories from the region's past, and enjoy sweeping views from the hilltop. The surrounding countryside also provides opportunities for walking and photography.
Quick Facts About Kunětická hora Castle
- Location: Near Pardubice, Bohemia, Czechia
- Type: Medieval castle and hilltop fortress
- Historical period: Late 14th or early 15th century
- Setting: An isolated volcanic hill above the Elbe lowlands
- Historical significance: A strategic stronghold expanded under the Pernštejn family
- Main highlights: Historic fortifications, castle towers, courtyards, and panoramic countryside views
- Things to do: Explore the castle, learn about Czech history, walk around the hill, and take photographs
- Best time to visit: Spring through autumn for pleasant weather and scenic views
Where Is Kunětická hora Castle?
Kunětická hora Castle stands on Kunětická hora hill, approximately a short drive from Pardubice in eastern Czechia. Its elevated position makes it a prominent landmark in the surrounding flat landscape. The castle is accessible by road from Pardubice and makes a worthwhile excursion for visitors exploring Bohemia's historic towns and countryside.

affa5ba8b65657ba1a5bfaea49c3f4878d257d07.content:
Kuneticka hora Castle
Kunětická hora Castle is one of the most distinctive landmarks of the Pardubice region. Rising above the surrounding countryside, the castle was built at the turn of the 15th and 16th centuries by the powerful Pernštejn family.
Today, visitors can explore the castle interiors and learn about its long and often dramatic history. The main tour route leads through the castle palace and includes access to the tower, which offers wide views of the surrounding landscape and the East Bohemian countryside.
Another exhibition is dedicated to the famous Czech architect Dušan Jurkovič, who played an important role in the restoration of the castle in the early 20th century.
Visitors can also see the Chapel of St. Catherine of Alexandria, featuring a Baroque altarpiece and preserved historic details.
Culture and events
Kunětická hora is not only a historic monument but also a lively cultural venue. During the summer months, the castle courtyard hosts theatre performances, concerts and festivals.
One of the highlights is the annual summer theatre stage of the East Bohemian Theatre Pardubice, which brings popular productions to the open-air setting of the castle. The area also hosts concerts and music festivals, including the well-known Czech Castles.CZ festival.
Throughout the year, the castle takes part in national heritage events such as European Heritage Days and Castle Night.
Special programmes and activities are often prepared for children, offering a playful introduction to medieval life. For opening hours, guided tours and current events, please visit the official castle website.

Rape statistics
| Rape | 
|---|
Statistics on rape and other acts of sexual assault are commonly available in industrialized countries, and have become better documented throughout the world. Inconsistent definitions of rape, different rates of reporting, recording, prosecution and conviction for rape can create controversial statistical disparities, and has led to concerns that many rape statistics may not accurately represent the extent of its prevalence.[1][2]
In some jurisdictions, male-on-female rape is the only form of rape counted in the statistics.[2] Some jurisdictions also don't count being forced to penetrate another as rape, creating further controversy around rape statistics.[3] Countries may not define marital rape (forced sex on a spouse) as rape.[4] Rape is an under-reported crime. The reasons for not reporting rape vary across countries, and may include fear of retaliation, uncertainty about whether a crime was committed or if the offender intended harm, feelings of shame or humiliation, not wanting the offender to get in trouble, fear of prosecution (e.g. due to laws against premarital sex), and doubt in or distrust of local law enforcement.[5][6]
In 2005, a United Nations statistical report compiled from government sources showed that more than 250,000 cases of rape or attempted rape were recorded by police annually. The reported data covered 65 countries.[7]
Research
[edit]
Most rape research and reporting to date has been limited to male–female forms of rape. Research on male–male and female–male is beginning to be done. However, almost no research has been done on female–female rape, though women can be charged with rape in a few jurisdictions. A few books, such as Violent Betrayal: Partner Abuse in Lesbian Relationships by Dr. Claire M. Renzetti,[9] No More Secrets: Violence in Lesbian Relationships by Janice Ristock,[10] and Woman-to-Woman Sexual Violence: Does She Call It Rape? by Lori B. Girshick[11] also cover the topic of rape of women by other women.

[edit]
This table indicates the annual number of recorded rapes per capita by country for last available year.[8] Each entry is based on that country's definition of rape, which varies widely throughout the world. It does not specify whether recorded means reported, brought to trial, or convicted. It does not include cases of rape which go unreported or unrecorded.[12][13] Alternative estimates can show large differences, such as South Africa having around 500,000 rapes per year (ten times the reported rate),[14] or Egypt having more than 20,000 rapes a year.[15]

George Pell (8 June 1941 – 10 January 2023) was an Australian cardinal of the Catholic Church. He was the inaugural prefect of the Secretariat for the Economy at the Vatican from 2014 to 2019 and a member of the Council of Cardinal Advisers from 2013 to 2018. Ordained a priest in 1966 and bishop in 1987, he was made a cardinal in 2003. Pell was the eighth Archbishop of Sydney (2001–2014), the seventh Archbishop of Melbourne (1996–2001) and an auxiliary bishop of Melbourne (1987–1996). He was also an author and columnist. As a conservative, Pell maintained a high public profile on a wide range of issues, while retaining an adherence to Catholic orthodoxy.
Pell worked as a priest in rural Victoria and in Melbourne and also chaired the aid organisation Caritas Australia (part of Caritas Internationalis) from 1988 to 1997. He was appointed a delegate to the Australian Constitutional Convention in 1998, received the Centenary Medal from the Australian government in 2003 and was appointed a Companion of the Order of Australia (AC) in the 2005 Queen's Birthday Honours. During his tenure as Archbishop of Melbourne, Pell set up the "Melbourne Response" protocol in 1996 to investigate and deal with complaints of child sexual abuse in the archdiocese. The protocol was the first of its kind in the world and was subjected to a variety of criticism.[1][2]
In 2018, Pell was convicted of sexually abusing a boy in Melbourne in the 1990s,[3][4][5] and served 404 days in prison, much of it in solitary confinement. On appeal the convictions were quashed and Pell acquitted in 2020 by the High Court of Australia in the decision Pell v The Queen.[6] A separate investigation by the Holy See's Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith into these allegations of abuse was concluded upon his acquittal by the High Court.[7] In 2025 it was announced that the National Redress Scheme, a non-judicial program, had accepted that Pell had sexually abused two boys in Ballarat in the 1970s, with compensation paid to one of those boys five weeks prior to Pell's death.[8][9][10][11]

c56476d85a8ab2c2b7ba4cac49ebf5a38968f959.content:
Agra:
 A special Pocso court in Agra has sentenced a 30-year-old man to life imprisonment on Tuesday for sexually assaulting a 12-year-old girl after abducting her from home while she was asleep.
The court also imposed a fine of Rs 50,000 on him. While delivering the verdict, special judge (Pocso) Sonika Chaudhary highlighted society’s failure to protect girls despite govt campaigns such as ‘Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao’.
According to prosecution, on the night of April 17, 2025, the girl’s father went out for work, leaving his daughter and three other children at home. Around 1am, the accused took his 12-year-old daughter to a garden outside the village, and violated her.
The girl was admitted to hospital for 10 days following the assault. Based on her father’s complaint, an FIR was filed at a police station in Agra under sections of 
rape
 and Pocso Act.
The convict, a father of two, has remained in jail since his arrest. During the trial, the prosecution examined 12 witnesses, including the complainant, the minor survivor, two doctors, ACP Gaurav Singh and inspector Inderjeet Singh.

c56476d85a8ab2c2b7ba4cac49ebf5a38968f959.title: Agra court sentences 2 to death for rape, murder of 5-year-old
c56476d85a8ab2c2b7ba4cac49ebf5a38968f959.content:
Agra court sentences 2 to death for rape, murder of 5-year-old
The verdict was delivered by Special Judge Sonika Chaudhary (ADJ-27), who stated that the crime had deeply disturbed the social conscience and warranted the maximum punishment under the law.
A special POCSO court in Agra has sentenced two men, Amit and Nikhil, to death for the abduction, sexual assault, and murder of a five-year-old girl in Farera village under Bah police station.
The verdict was delivered by Special Judge Sonika Chaudhary (ADJ-27), who stated that the crime had deeply disturbed the social conscience and warranted the maximum punishment under the law.
The incident took place on 18 March 2024, when the child was playing near a canal outside her home. According to Assistant District Government Counsel (Crime) Subhash Giri, who prosecuted the case along with colleague Vijeta Selwania, "The complainant's five-year-old daughter was playing near the village canal. From there, she was taken away by the accused, Amit and Nikhil, on a motorcycle after luring her. After that, they committed brutal sexual assault on her, both natural and unnatural. They inflicted multiple injuries all over her body, and later murdered her in a gruesome manner."
Following the crime, on 19 March, the accused called the victim's father and demanded Rs 6 lakh in ransom. Giri explained, "Based on the details of that phone call, the accused were arrested on March 20 and 21. On the basis of their confession and disclosure, the victim's body was recovered."
The postmortem confirmed sexual assault and multiple injuries. The police filed the chargesheet within 20-25 days, registering the case under IPC Sections 363 (kidnapping), 364A (kidnapping for ransom), 302 (murder), 201 (causing disappearance of evidence), and 376 (rape), along with Sections 5M/6 and 5G/6 of the POCSO Act.
"The trial in this case commenced immediately in the Hon'ble Court," Giri said. "During the trial, the prosecution presented 18 witnesses in total. All evidence clearly proved the case beyond doubt, and the Hon'ble Court, after examining all facts, today convicted both accused and awarded them the death penalty."
Giri added, "I am deeply thankful to the Hon'ble Court for delivering such a strong and just judgment in this matter."
The victim's mother, reacting to the verdict, said, "Had they remained alive, who knows how many more would have suffered?"

751333e7f849287ec9974f6a4334bef4a8a1edbf.content:
List of serial killers in the United States
A serial killer is typically a person who murders three or more people, with the murders taking place over more than a month and including a significant period of time between them.[1][2] The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) defines serial murder as "a series of two or more murders, committed as separate events, usually, but not always, by one offender acting alone".[2][3]
The United States has by far the largest number of documented serial killers in the world. According to Radford University's Serial Killer Information Center, it has more documented serial killers than the next ten highest countries on the list combined.[4]
Identified serial killers
[edit]
| Name | Years active | Proven victims | Possible victims | Fate | Notes | Ref. | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ables, Tony | 1970–1990 | 4 | 4+ | Sentenced to life imprisonment | Murdered robbery victim; paroled and later killed at least three women in St. Petersburg, Florida | [5][6] | 
| Acevedo, Francisco | 1989–1996 | 3 | 3 | Sentenced to 75 years to life | Strangled three prostitutes in New York between 1989 and 1996 | [7] | 
| Adams, Edward James | 1920–1921 | 7 | 7 | Killed by police | Murdered seven people, including three policemen | [8] | 
| Adams, Stanley Theodore | 1999 | 3 | 5+ | Sentenced to death | Murdered three people between August and October 1999, and suspected for at least two more killings | [9] |

| Albanese, Charles | 1980–1981 | 3 | 3 | Executed 1995 | Poisoned family members with arsenic in Fox Lake, Illinois to receive their inheritance | [11] | 
| Alcala, Rodney | 1971–1979 | 8 | 50–130+ | Died in prison awaiting execution | Sometimes called "The Dating Game Killer" because of his 1978 appearance on the television show The Dating Game in the midst of his murder spree | [12] | 
| Alix, Franklin DeWayne | 1997–1998 | 4 | 4 | Executed 2010 | Murdered people in Houston, Texas, during robberies | [13] | 
| Allen, Herman | 1930–1942 | 4 | 4 | Executed 1942 | Killed a lodger in 1930; after release, he killed three more people in a fit of jealousy | [14] | 
| Allen, Howard | 1974–1987 | 3 | 3 | Died in prison | Targeted elderly victims during burglaries in Indiana | [15][16] |

Denis Georges Waxin (born 26 June 1968) is a French serial killer and serial rapist who attacked at least six children in Lille and its suburbs from 1985 to 1999, killing three girls, raping two boys and another girl. He was convicted for his proven crimes and sentenced to life imprisonment with 29 years of preventative detention.[1]
Early life
[edit]
Denis Georges Waxin was born on 26 June 1968, in Loos, Nord, but spent his childhood in Wattignies. His parents had a strained relationship, as his mother Marie-Jeanne spent most of her time working, while his strict father never spoke to him and preferred to spend his time gambling. As he was given no affection from most of his other four siblings, with the sole exception of his older brother Dominique, Waxin grew up lonely and isolated from others around him.
In 1985, Waxin became depressed when Dominique, now an adult, left the family home. In an attempt to take his mind off his troubles, he began to take walks by himself every day for hours on end.
Attacks
[edit]
On the late afternoon of 22 November 1985, 7-year-old Nathalie Hoareau was sent to buy cigarettes and bread for her mother from the local store, but on the way, she was approached by Waxin, who offered to show her his shack.[2] After Hoareau followed him to a vacant lot, Waxin raped the girl and attempted to strangle her with the candy necklace she wore around her neck, before ultimately stabbing her twice in the heart. Later that night, the concerned mother notified the police about the disappearance, which led them to discover the little girl's body in a bush. She had been left completely naked, with a pack of cigarettes and a shopping list with a written message to her mother beside the body. Traces of semen were also located on the body, but since most of it was washed away by the rain, authorities were unable to establish a genetic profile.[2]
In July 1986, Waxin obtained a diploma in carpentry and was stationed in Germany as part of his military service in 1989. While on leave, he began a short-lived relationship with an older woman, which lasted until the end of service in August 1990. Shortly afterwards, he fell into depression again.
On 8 October 1990, 9-year-old Cathy Monchaux was playing in the garden of the family home in Wazemmes when her father called to go inside.[2] Before she could do that, however, Waxin approached her and offered to buy her candy. Monchaux agreed and followed him to an abandoned soccer field, where she was raped and stabbed fourteen times after a failed escape attempt.[3] When she failed to return home, her parents and older sister went out to look for her, and after an hour of searching, they called the police. On the following day, Monchaux's naked body was found by a man walking his dog.[2]
Shortly after this crime, Waxin fell in love with another woman, whom he subsequently married and went to live with in an apartment in Moulins. Neither of them wanted children, and Waxin called his wife "Mom". He was described as helpful, charming and a good husband, and eventually managed to find a job at an Auchan service station in Villeneuve-d'Ascq. While regarded as punctual and conscientious, Waxin was also considered unpredictable - on one occasion, he emptied the magazine of an alarm pistol while aiming it at a thief. He would eventually be fired for threatening to set fire to the station because his boss had reprimanded him.[4]
On the late afternoon of 23 July 1992, 4-year-old Nadjia Thebib was playing with other children in front of a dilapidated building where her grandmother, Meriem, lived,
